title: Greek Philosophical Foundations
summary: Socrates, Plato and Aristotle on the soul, knowledge and the mind–body relation; dualism versus monism; the legacy of Greek rationalism and empiricism for later psychological science.

notes.t: Socrates focused on the soul and moral virtues and argued that truth is uncovered through questioning — the Socratic dialogue or elenctic method, a form of dialectic involving questioning and dialogue to stimulate critical thinking and illuminate ideas. This method emphasised rationalism, asserting that through reasoned discourse, individuals could uncover inherent truths. Socrates did not write; his ideas survive through Plato. He is commonly credited with laying groundwork for later mind–body dualism.

Plato, a student of Socrates, held the Theory of Forms: the material world is a shadow of an eternal, unchanging realm of ideal forms. For Plato, the soul is immaterial and pre-exists the body; knowledge is recollection (anamnesis) of the forms the soul knew before embodiment — a rationalist and nativist position.

Plato's dualism proposes that mind and body are fundamentally different substances — a view later developed by Descartes. Plato's key ideas include knowledge as innate and accessed by reasoning, the Chariot Allegory (white and black horse — higher versus lower self) and the Cave Allegory (people accept their own version of reality).

Aristotle, a student of Plato, rejected the Theory of Forms. He argued that form and matter are united in individual things, that the mind at birth is a blank slate (tabula rasa), and that knowledge comes through experience and the senses — an early empiricist position.

Aristotle's approach embodies empiricism, asserting that knowledge arises from sensory experiences and evidence gathered from the natural world. His key contribution was formal logic and the syllogism — a form of deductive reasoning where conclusions are drawn from two premises (e.g., all men are mortal; Ram is a man; therefore Ram is mortal).

r: Mind and body are fundamentally different substances
Reality consists only of the physical body; the mind is not a separate substance
Mind and body emerge from a common neutral substance

notes.t: Plato believed the soul existed before birth and was separate from the body — an example of classical dualism. Aristotle rejected this, focusing on the physical world and adopting a monist metaphysics with an empiricist epistemology.

Plato = nativism and dualism; Aristotle = tabula rasa and empiricism; Socrates = elenctic (questioning) method. These positions are frequently contrasted in matching and assertion–reasoning questions.
